title: your grandmother before dinner
hook: your grandmother before dinner; a gift you didn't earn

segments.voice: Picture a kitchen table. The food is on it, steam coming off the potatoes, and somebody's already reaching for the bread. And then a hand on the wrist. Your grandmother, or someone's grandmother, saying: wait. Grace first. Heads go down. A few quick words, a quick amen, and then everybody eats. Millions of families have done this every night of their lives, and most kids at that table thought grace meant the little speech before dinner. It does. But the word is much bigger than the speech. It's the reason for the speech. Today's word is the first one on this path, and in a sense every other word sits on top of it.
screen: `A KITCHEN TABLE.` → `WAIT. GRACE FIRST.` → `THE WORD IS BIGGER THAN THE SPEECH.`

segments.voice: Grace comes from the Latin word gratia. It means a favor. A gift. Something given freely, not paid for. It's the same root that gives English the word gratitude, and the word gratis, meaning free of charge. The New Testament was written in Greek, and there the word is charis, which also means a gift freely given, and a kind of loveliness. So when Catholics talk about grace, they mean God's gift of himself, given before anybody earned it. The letter to the Ephesians says it plainly, in the old Douay-Rheims Bible that English-speaking Catholics used for centuries: "For by grace you are saved through faith, and that not of yourselves, for it is the gift of God." Not of yourselves. That's the surprise at the heart of the word. You don't climb up to grace. It comes down to you. Catholics say it arrives in many ways: in baptism, in the sacraments, in prayer, in an ordinary Tuesday when a friend calls at exactly the right moment. And here's where the dinner table comes back in. The old grace many Catholic families say goes like this: "Bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts, which we are about to receive from thy bounty, through Christ our Lord. Amen." Listen to what it notices. Thy gifts. Thy bounty. The food on the table is a small picture of the big thing. Somebody grew it, somebody cooked it, and before any of that, Catholics say, somebody gave the world to begin with. So saying grace isn't paying a fee before eating. It's noticing that you were given something. That's the whole shape of today's word: a gift you didn't earn, and the moment you notice it.
screen: `GRATIA — A FAVOR, A GIFT.` · `CHARIS — GIVEN FREELY.` · `NOT OF YOURSELVES.` · `THE TABLE IS A SMALL PICTURE.` · then, large: `A GIFT YOU DIDN'T EARN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice for day one, and it's small on purpose. One breath, with the bell. Before you breathe, think of one thing you have today that you didn't earn. The air, maybe. A person. A roof. Then breathe in slowly, all the way, and let it out. If you pray, you can say thank you with that breath. If you don't, just let yourself notice the gift.
Grace. A favor, a gift freely given. Catholics say it comes first, before anyone earns it. First word on your strand.
screen: `GRACE — your 1st word` → clicks onto an empty word-strand.

segments.voice: Your line to carry: you are already held. Grace means the gift came first. Today, before one meal, even a snack at your desk, pause for a single second and notice that it was given to you. That's day one. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Many Catholic families say a short grace before meals, often the traditional "Bless us, O Lord," and many make the sign of the cross before and after it.
